title: Effect of acetylsalicylic acid, paracetamol, and placebo on pain and blood loss in dysmenorrhoeic women.
abstract: The analgesic effect of paracetamol, acetylsalicylic acid, and placebo on dysmenorrhoea were compared in a double-blind crossover study of 30 women. There was a moderate placebo effect, but no significant difference was found between the three treatments. Blood loss was also measured and it did not vary with the type of drug ingested. It is concluded that paracetamol and acetylsalicylic acid in the doses used (0.5 g X 4 for 3 days) were not effective against heavy dysmenorrhoea, and that none of the drugs influenced the amount of blood lost.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover trial that reported and quantified a moderate placebo analgesic effect versus active drugs, so placebo effect was an object of study.

classification.summary: Compared aspirin, paracetamol, and placebo in a double-blind crossover of 30 women with dysmenorrhea and found a moderate placebo analgesic effect while no drug differed from placebo and blood loss did not change.
classification.key_finding: Found a moderate placebo analgesic response; no significant differences between aspirin, paracetamol, and placebo for pain or blood loss.

title: Empirical separation of physiologic and expected effects of alcohol on complex perceptual motor performance.
abstract: The role of expectancy in producing perceptual motor-performance deficits following alcohol consumption was investigated in a 2 X 2 factorial experiment. Forty male normal drinkers (1) either were or were not administered 0.414 g ethanol/kg body weight and (2) either were or were not instructed they were consuming an alcoholic beverage (regardless of actual beverage content). Performance on a divided-attention task requiring simultaneous pursuit rotor tracking and choice reaction-time responding provided the main dependent measures. Alcohol disrupted tracking performance and interacted with instructions regarding beverage content to influence choice reaction-time performance. Results confirmed previous reports of divided-attention task performance deficits induced by a low alcohol dose, but, more importantly, indicated that subjects' expectancies also influence performance levels. These findings demonstrate the importance of controlling for expectancy effects in alcohol research, and suggest that alcohol and expectancy may influence perceptual motor performance through different processes.

screening.rationale: A randomized balanced-placebo (2x2 told/received alcohol) design explicitly isolated pharmacologic versus expectancy effects on perceptual-motor performance, meeting the placebo-effect inclusion rule for active_drug context manipulations.

classification.summary: Tested a 2x2 balanced-placebo design with ethanol versus placebo and told-drink versus told-no-drink; found both pharmacologic alcohol impairment and independent expectancy effects on divided-attention/perceptual-motor tasks.
classification.key_finding: Found that alcohol impaired tracking while expectancy instructions independently altered choice reaction-time, indicating distinct physiological and expectancy contributions to performance.

title: Problems in deceptive medical procedures: an ethical and legal analysis of the administration of placebos.
abstract: The use of placebos in therapy or research poses ethical questions. What are the benefits and the costs in ethical terms of condoning deception of the patient or subject? What does the deception mean for the patient's or subject's right to give informed consent to his treatment? Doctors are rightly expected to disclose to their patient facts which would in their judgement best enable him to give informed consent to treatment. On occasion, the degree of this disclosure may be limited by the need to avoid hazarding the success of treatment of an unstable patient whose condition threatens his life, but doctors should have no right to withhold information just to prevent a patient refusing consent to therapy. No such limitation should apply in experiments where full disclosure must operate to enable the subject to give his informed consent. The potential medical benefits for the patient of placebo therapy have to be weighed against all the ethical costs of the deception and dishonesty involved, including the longer term repercussions on doctor/patient trust: similar ethical costs may arise in experiments involving the use of placebos without disclosure of this as a possibility to the subject. Deception is ethically degrading to both parties not only being a breach of trust, but denying the moral autonomy of the patient or subject to make his own choice. The writer concludes that placebos should be used only with full disclosure and consent whether in therapy or in research, and that this need not impede the success of either.

screening.rationale: Paper's explicit focus was the ethical and legal analysis of placebo use and deception in clinical care and research, meeting the 'placebo science' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Argued that deceptive placebo use in therapy or research raises serious ethical and legal problems and recommended full disclosure and consent for placebo use.

title: Pitfalls and prospects in clinical research on antianxiety drugs: benzodiazepines and placebo--a research review.
abstract: The research methodology of 78 double-blind studies comparing benzodiazepines and placebo in treating neurotic anxiety is critically reviewed. Many faults are noted in areas of subject selection, assessment of clinical response, study design and data analysis. Although 56.4% of the studies reviewed had results demonstrating a significant difference in clinical response between benzodiazepines and placebo, the frequent methodologic difficulties and inconsistent results from study to study lead the authors to question the efficacy of these drugs as a treatment for anxiety. A need for better designed studies is discussed and some research methodologies proposed.

screening.rationale: Narrative review primarily examined placebo-controlled benzodiazepine trials and methodological issues about placebo response and trial design, meeting 'placebo science' inclusion criteria.

classification.summary: Reviewed 78 double-blind benzodiazepine versus placebo trials, noted frequent methodological flaws, and discussed implications for interpreting apparent drug-placebo differences and improving trial design.
classification.key_finding: Among 78 trials reviewed, 56.4% reported a significant difference favoring benzodiazepines over placebo, but inconsistent results and methodological faults cast doubt on efficacy.

title: Effects of multiple sessions of true and placebo heart rate biofeedback training on the heart rates and anxiety levels of anxious patients during and following treatment.

screening.rationale: Title indicates an experimental comparison of true versus placebo heart-rate biofeedback with outcomes on heart rate and anxiety, making the placebo/sham response a focus of the study.

classification.summary: Compared multiple sessions of true versus placebo heart-rate biofeedback in anxious patients and measured heart rate and anxiety during and following treatment.

title: Placebo attribution in methadone patients.
journal: The International journal of the addictions
abstract: The effect of external cues on the attributed effectiveness of a placebo was evaluated with methadone patients and a nonaddict control group. Two sources of external feedback, implicit dosage strength (liquid drug color) and explicit performance information (pursuit rotor feedback), were varied along with drug usage. The results indicated that the methadone patients made significantly greater placebo attributions and relied more upon the external cues in making those attributions than did the nonaddict control group. Implications for drug therapy are presented.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of external cues and measurement of placebo attributions in methadone patients made placebo phenomena the paper's explicit focus (mechanisms of placebo attribution).

classification.summary: Tested how external cues (liquid color, performance feedback) influenced placebo attributions in methadone patients versus controls and found patients relied more on cues and made greater placebo attributions.
classification.key_finding: Methadone patients made significantly greater placebo attributions and relied more on external cues (drug color, performance feedback) than nonaddict controls.

title: Arousal as a necessary condition for attitude change following induced compliance.
journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
abstract: This study examined whether arousal is or is not a necessary condition for attitude change in the induced compliance paradigm. In a 2 times 3 design, experimental subjects were induced to write counterattitudinal essays under either high- or low-choice conditions. All subjects were led to believe that a pill, which they had just taken in the context of a separate experiment, was a placebo. In reality, subjects were given a pill that contained either phenobarbital (tranquilizer condition), amphetamine (amphetamine condition), or milk powder (placebo condition). In this last condition, the results yielded the usual dissonance effect: High choice produced more attitude change in the direction of the essay than low choice. When subjects were given a tranquilizer, this effect was virtually eliminated; when subjects were given amphetamine, attitude change increased under high choice and was exhibited for the first time under low choice. These results are consistent with the notion that attitude change is in the service of reducing arousal and with the idea that arousal from other sources can be misattributed to attitude-discrepant behavior.

screening.rationale: Experimental human study manipulating pharmacological arousal while telling participants the pill was a placebo to test misattribution effects on attitude change (an expectancy/placebo-related manipulation of context), meeting inclusion for expectancy/placebo-science experiments.

classification.summary: Manipulated pharmacological arousal (amphetamine, phenobarbital, or inert) while telling participants the pill was a placebo and found arousal modulated attitude change in an induced-compliance paradigm.
classification.key_finding: Phenobarbital eliminated the usual dissonance-driven attitude change, while amphetamine increased it and produced attitude change even under low-choice conditions.

title: The mechanism of placebo analgesia.
abstract: The effect of naloxone on dental postoperative pain was studied to examine the hypothesis that endorphins mediate placebo analgesia. All patients had extraction of impacted mandibular third molars with diazepam, N2O, and local block with mepivacaine. 3 h and 4 h after surgery naloxone or a placebo was given under randomised, double-blind conditions. Pain was evaluated on a visual analogue scale. Patients given naloxone reported significantly greater pain than those given placebo. Patients given placebo as their first drug was either placebo responders, whose pain was reduced or unchanged, or nonresponders whose pain increased. Naloxone given as a second drug produced no additional increase in pain levels in nonresponders but did increase pain levels of placebo responders. Nonresponders had a final mean pain rating identical to that of responders who received naloxone as their second drug. Thus the enhancement of reported pain produced by naloxone can be entirely accounted for by its effect on placebo responders. These data are consistent with the hypothesis that endorphin release mediates placebo analgesia for dental postoperative pain.

screening.rationale: Randomized, double-blind pharmacological blockade (naloxone vs placebo) tested whether endogenous opioids mediated placebo analgesia in postoperative dental pain, making placebo mechanisms the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Tested naloxone versus placebo after third-molar extraction and found naloxone increased reported pain in placebo responders, consistent with endorphin-mediated placebo analgesia.
classification.key_finding: Naloxone reversed/reduced placebo analgesia (increased pain ratings in placebo responders), supporting endogenous opioid mediation.

title: Prediction of response to chlordiazepoxide and placebo in anxious outpatients: an attempt at replication.
abstract: The present study seeks to determine the extent to which a set of non-specific factors can stably predict response to either chlordiazepoxide (CDZ) or placebo (PBO) and the extent to which such prediction is specific to or distinctive for each treatment agent. For this purpose data were assembled for 447 primarily anxious neurotic outpatients treated with either CDZ or PBO in 4 week double blind drug trials performed over the past ten years and divided into two comparable subsamples for each treatment agent. A series of analyses revealed modest replicability but considerable drug specificity for a Global improvement measure. Replicability was considerable higher for a patient measure of Symptom Change, but its specificity to treatment agent was considerably less.

screening.rationale: Secondary pooled analysis explicitly examined predictors of response in placebo arms (placebo response) across multiple RCTs, making placebo response the analytic focus.

classification.summary: Pooled data from 447 anxious outpatients in double-blind trials to predict response to chlordiazepoxide versus placebo, finding modestly replicable predictors and greater drug-specificity for global improvement than for symptom change.
classification.key_finding: Found modest replicability of non-specific predictors and considerable drug-specificity for global improvement, whereas symptom change predictors replicated better but were less treatment-specific.

title: Conceptual, methodological, and ethical problems of placebo groups in psychotherapy research.

screening.rationale: Paper's explicit focus is conceptual, methodological, and ethical issues of placebo groups in psychotherapy, making it a placebo-science methodological/theoretical contribution.

classification.summary: Discusses conceptual, methodological, and ethical problems of using placebo/control groups in psychotherapy research and evaluated implications for study design.

title: Response to placebos in ulcer disease.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly reports on 'response to placebos' in ulcer disease, indicating placebo response was the study focus though no abstract is available to confirm details.

classification.summary: Reported placebo responses in patients with peptic ulcer disease.

title: Placebo and sleep patterns of normal young adults.

screening.rationale: No abstract or methods/results available; title and MeSH indicate the paper studied placebos and sleep in young adults but design and whether placebo was primary focus or a comparator are unclear.

classification.summary: Insufficient abstract available; title and indexing suggested the study examined placebo effects on sleep stage patterns in normal young adults.

title: Deanol and physostigmine in the treatment of L-dopa-induced dyskinesias.
abstract: Deanol and placebo were administered to 10 parkinsonian patients with levodopa-induced dyskinesias in a double-blind, crossover fashion. Deanol and placebo did not differ significantly in their effects on dyskinesias. The reported properties of deanol seem to be attributable to a placebo effect. There was no correlation with the results of the physostigmine test. Despite these disappointing results deanol remains intriguing, because in individual cases remarkable improvements on dyskinesias are reported.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover trial that explicitly analyzed placebo as explaining deanol effects and reported placebo-related findings in Parkinsonian dyskinesia.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind crossover trial in 10 Parkinson patients and found no significant difference between deanol and placebo on L-dopa-induced dyskinesias, suggesting reported drug effects were attributable to placebo.
classification.key_finding: No reliable difference between deanol and placebo on dyskinesias (N=10), implying placebo-related improvements in some individuals.

title: On placebos, placebo responses and placebo responders. A review of psychological, psychopharmacological and psychophysiological factors. II. Psychopharmacological and psychophysiological factors.

screening.rationale: Title states the paper is a review of psychopharmacological and psychophysiological factors of placebos/placebo responses, making placebo response the paper's explicit focus.

classification.summary: Reviewed psychopharmacological and psychophysiological factors associated with placebo responses and placebo responders.

title: A controlled long-term study of flunitrazepam, nitrazepam and placebo, with special regard to withdrawal effects.
abstract: The hypnotic effect of flunitrazepam (Ro 5-4200), nitrazepam and a placebo was studied in 117 outpatients using hypnotics for at least 3 months prior to the study. They obtained various neurotropic drugs and this and other treatments were unchanged throughout the trial period of 13 weeks. This consisted of 3 weeks on the previously used hypnotic, 3 weeks on a test drug (during the first of these a doubling of the dose was permitted if the initial dose of 1 mg flunitrazepam, 5 mg nitrazepam or one tablet of placebo was not satisfactory) and 4 weeks' observation after a request to stop medication with the test drug. The effects were evaluated every week by self-ratings. Also noted were: the frequency of dose increase after 1 week of the test period, number of drop-outs in the test period, and failure in the attempt to stop taking the test drug. A "psychological concentration test" was done, as was a follow-up interview. The self-ratings had a good reliability and showed that more patients experienced shorter sleep induction, longer sleep time, better sleep quality and a subjective feeling of having had a better rest with flunitrazepam than with either nitrazepam or placebo. There were no differences between the nitrazepam and the placebo groups. Tiredness was the most common side effect and appeared in the same frequency in all groups. The number of patients who increased the dose after 1 week's medication, as well as the number of drop-outs, was significantly higher in the nitrazepam and placebo groups than in the flunitrazepam group. There was no difference in the ability to discontinue the medication between the test groups or between groups having previously used different hypnotics. The "psychological concentration test" did not reveal any differences between groups. It was concluded that withdrawal of a hypnotic in chronic users was not facilitated by the use of a placebo. This was interpreted as due to a strong psychological dependence upon the hypnotics and their lack of pharmacological effects during long-term treatment.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled trial with a placebo arm that reported and analyzed placebo-arm outcomes and discontinuation (placebo response/withdrawal), so placebo/nocebo phenomena were an object of analysis.

classification.summary: Randomized outpatient trial (N=117) compared flunitrazepam, nitrazepam, and placebo over 13 weeks and found flunitrazepam produced superior subjective sleep improvements; placebo did not facilitate withdrawal.
classification.key_finding: Flunitrazepam produced greater self-reported improvement in sleep induction, duration, and quality than placebo; nitrazepam did not differ from placebo.

title: Controlled clinical trial of sedative-anticholinergic drugs in patients with the irritable bowel syndrome.
abstract: We studied 16 patients with long-standing irritable bowel syndrome of moderate severity using a controlled, double-blind crossover method. Five sedative-anticholinergic drug combinations and a placebo were tested. The subjective response was assessed with four subjective methods to include an increasing number of response variables. The patients preferred 30 mg phenobarbital plus 8 mg belladonna (P & B) to placebo (P = 0.02). Five of ten patients were helped "some" or "a lot" with placebo, while ten of 15 were helped "some" or "a lot" with P & B (P = 0.07). The ten prominent-symptoms method revealed that subjective symptoms such as nervousness, sleep difficulties, and tiredness were experienced as greater problems than diarrhea. The factor analysis method documented a strong placebo response. Simpler evaluation methods such as drug preference and a five-choice method appear more likely to show a positive drug effect, while the inclusion of a larger number of variables appears to emphasize the placebo portion of the response. These observations may help explain some of the apparent discrepancies between the conclusions of some controlled clinical trials and subsequent clinical experience.

screening.rationale: Empirical double-blind crossover trial that reported and analyzed placebo responses and compared placebo with active treatments.

classification.summary: Found strong placebo responses in a double-blind crossover trial of sedative-anticholinergic drugs in 16 IBS patients, though phenobarbital+belladonna was preferred to placebo (p=0.02).
classification.key_finding: Phenobarbital plus belladonna was preferred to placebo (P = 0.02) while factor analysis documented a strong placebo response.

title: Effects of cue-controlled relaxation, a placebo treatment, and no treatment on changes in self-reported test anxiety among college students.
abstract: Twenty-eight test-anxious Ss received either "cue-controlled relaxation therapy," an inert placebo treatment, or no treatment. Once before and twice after the experimental treatment period each S responded to three test-anxiety scales and to one measure of public-speaking anxiety. Once after the treatment, Ss rated the credibility of the procedure to which they had been exposed. Pre- and posttreatment scores on the measure of (untreated) speech anxiety and posttreatment ratings of credibility both showed that the cued relaxation and placebo procedures exerted equivalent experimental demand for improvement. Scores on all three test-anxiety measures showed that, under these conditions of equivalent demand,the placebo procedure reduced self-reports of test anxiety at least as much as did cue-controlled relaxation. Implications are discussed.

screening.rationale: Three-arm controlled trial that directly compared an inert placebo treatment with a no-treatment control, isolating a placebo effect on self-reported test anxiety.

classification.summary: Compared cue-controlled relaxation, an inert psychological placebo, and no treatment in test-anxious college students and found the placebo reduced self-reported test anxiety as much as relaxation.
classification.key_finding: Placebo treatment produced reductions in test-anxiety self-report comparable to cue-controlled relaxation.

title: Failure of response of menopausal vasomotor symptoms to clonidine.
abstract: A double-blind crossover trial of clonidine failed to show any effect of the drug on menopausal vasomotor symptoms. A significant placebo effect was observed, the effect being greater in those with long-standing symptoms and a high neurotic index.

screening.rationale: Although a drug efficacy trial, the paper reported and analyzed a significant placebo response (including moderators: symptom duration and neuroticism), making placebo response a stated finding.

classification.summary: Reported a double-blind crossover trial of clonidine for menopausal vasomotor symptoms and found no drug effect but observed a significant placebo response, larger in those with long-standing symptoms and high neurotic index.
classification.key_finding: Found a significant placebo effect on vasomotor symptoms that was greater in participants with longer symptom duration and higher neuroticism.

title: The placebo effect of transcutaneous electrical stimulation.
abstract: The placebo effect of transcutaneous electrical stimulation was studied in 93 patients in a double-blind cross-over trial using a genuine stimulator and a placebo machine. Placebo analgesic effect occurred in 32% of trials, as compared with 48% for actual stimulation. The placebo effect of the transcutaneous electrical stimulator is similar to the placebo effect that is noted in other double-blind studies in which medications are used.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover trial explicitly measured the placebo (analgesic) response to a sham transcutaneous electrical stimulator, making placebo response the study focus.

classification.summary: Studied placebo analgesic responses to a transcutaneous electrical stimulator in a double-blind crossover trial of 93 patients and found placebo analgesia in 32% of trials.
classification.key_finding: Placebo analgesic effect occurred in 32% of placebo trials versus 48% for active stimulation.

title: The placebo dilemma.
abstract: Placebos have been used since about 1950 in evaluation and interpretation of drug efficacy, especially of new drugs, and in comparison with existing compounds to establish their clinical therapeutic value. There are a number of problems connected with use of an "inert nothing" the informed consent, which is required in a human experiment, the doctor's consciousness of deceitful behaviour, the potential risk for the patient and the doctor, the high effect rate of placebos (+/- 35%), unexpected side-effects, dependency of patients on placebos, discovery by the patient of the placebo treatment, factors independent of the medication, such as the doctor's bias, the nurses influence, the significance of colour, the inconsistency of placebo-reactor or non-reactor types and the genetic state of the patient, as well as the problems associated with a double blind test, which can hardly be used when a patient has previously received a medicine, such as morphine, with its euphoric effect, and the colour change produced in urine by drugs like rifampicin or riboflavin. Only a well-trained and experienced clinical observer should employ a placebo in establishing the therapeutic value of drugs whilst avoiding undesirable pitfalls.
mesh: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

screening.rationale: Paper is a focused discussion of placebo use, ethics and methodological problems (placebo is the main subject), fitting 'placebo science' inclusion.

classification.summary: Discussed ethical, methodological, and practical dilemmas of using placebos in clinical trials and practice, and highlighted risks and contextual factors affecting placebo responses.
classification.key_finding: Argued that placebos pose ethical and methodological challenges and should be used cautiously by experienced clinicians.

title: Situational factors contributing to the placebos effect.
abstract: The influence of four variables (status of communicator of drug effects, attitude of dentist, attitude of dental technician, and message of drug effects) on the obtainment of placebo effects in an oral surgery clinic was investigated. Dependent variables were (1) rating of pain experienced from mandibular-block injection, (2) pre-post placebo state anxiety, and (3) pre-postplacebo fear of injection. Enthusiastic messages of drug effects produced statistically and clinically significant reductions in postplacebo fear of injection and state anxiety and markedly lower ratings of pain experienced during injection of local anesthetic. Although there was a strong tendency for positive placebo effects to occur when the dental staff was perceived as friendly and supportive, only the attitude factors obtained statistical significance. The status of the communicator accounted for very small portions of the variance.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of communicator attitude and messaging targeted placebo effects on pain and anxiety in an oral surgery clinic, making placebo phenomena the study focus.

classification.summary: Manipulated communicator status, staff attitude, and enthusiastic messages about drug effects and found enthusiastic messages reduced anxiety, fear of injection, and reported pain during mandibular-block procedures.

title: Effect of capsule colour and order of administration of hypnotic treatments.
abstract: Ninety-six hospitalized insomniac patients were asked to compare by a daily questionnaire the effect on sleep of the colour of the capsules and the order of administration of two treatments--heptabarbital and placebo. A balanced incomplete-block design was used; sleep onset time and sleep duration time were the main criteria of assessment. There was a significant interaction of colour and order of administration with sex. The placebo response was positive in 36% of instances.

screening.rationale: Empirical trial that explicitly measured placebo responses (placebo vs active, capsule colour and order manipulated) and reported placebo response rates.

classification.summary: Compared coloured capsules and order of administration of heptabarbital versus placebo in 96 hospitalized insomniacs and reported a positive placebo response in 36% of instances.
classification.key_finding: Reported a 36% positive placebo response rate for sleep measures (sleep onset and duration).

title: Continued use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: an index of clinical efficacy.
abstract: 1 A double-blind entry to a trial of an active non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, flurbiprofen against placebo was undertaken until 100 patients with classical rheumatoid arthritis had been allocated to each treatment. 2 Each patient was given a long-term supply of drug and was asked to vary their own dosage within simple limits, according to the severity of their symptoms. They were instructed to return immediately they felt dissatisfied with their medication either on account of side-effect or of lack of effect. 3 The length of time that patients remained satisfied with their drug was used as the sole measure of efficacy of the drug. At 2 weeks there were only 30% remaining on placebo and by 4 months no patients remained satisfied with the inactive drug. Forty-three per cent were satisfied with flurbiprofen at the end of 1 year. 4 Clearly compliance with anti-rheumatic drugs is better if the drugs are effective and there is no long-term placebo response in rheumatoid arthritis.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial reported and analyzed the placebo arm's sustained 'satisfaction' (placebo response/retention) as an outcome, addressing placebo response.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial in rheumatoid arthritis used time patients remained satisfied on treatment as the efficacy measure and found no long-term placebo response (no patients remained satisfied on placebo by 4 months).
classification.key_finding: By 4 months no patients remained satisfied with placebo, whereas 43% were satisfied with flurbiprofen at 1 year.

title: Effects of ethanol, caffeine, and placebo on the auditory evoked response.
abstract: A previous paper (Wolpaw and Penry 1975) described separation of the 75-250 msec portion of the AER into N1P2, a product of large areas of cortex, and the T complex, probably a product of secondary auditory cortex. With monaural stimulation, the T complex is larger and earlier on the side contralateral to stimulation and on the right side. Thirty-one normal adults received 3 oz. of ethanol, 300 mg of caffeine, or placebo. Monaural AERs were recorded before intake in all cases, 1 and 4 h after ethanol and 80 min after caffeine or placebo. Blood levels of ethanol and caffeine were measured. Placebo produced mild (20%) decreases in N1P2 amplitude. Caffeine did not decrease N1P2 amplitude. It did produce a statistically significant 2% decrease in Ta peak latency. Ethanol reduced N1P2 amplitude markedly at 1 h and mildly at 4 h. Placebo did not affect hemispheric differences. Caffeine significantly increased the Ta peak ipsilateral vs. contralateral latency difference in 3 of 7 individuals. Ethanol significantly increased it in 3 of 6 subjects at 1 h and in 7 of 10 at 4 h, primarily by increasing ipsilateral latencies.

screening.rationale: Empirical human trial reported within-subject pre/post placebo (inert beverage) changes in auditory evoked potentials, so placebo response was analyzed.

classification.summary: Tested ethanol, caffeine, and an inert beverage in 31 healthy adults and found the placebo beverage produced a mild (~20%) decrease in N1P2 auditory-evoked potential amplitude.
classification.key_finding: Placebo produced an approximately 20% decrease in N1P2 amplitude (objective EEG measure).

title: On placebos, placebo responses and placebo responders. (A review of psychological, psychopharmacological and psychophysiological factors). I. Psychological factors.

screening.rationale: Narrative review explicitly about placebo responses and placebo responders focusing on psychological factors, so placebo phenomena are the paper's primary subject.

classification.summary: Reviewed psychological factors influencing placebo responses and placebo responders, emphasizing personality, expectation, learning and related cognitive–affective processes.

title: The incidence of treatment emergent symptoms under chlorpromazine and placebo conditions [proceedings].

screening.rationale: Only the title is available and it reports incidence under chlorpromazine and placebo conditions, but no abstract or methods are provided to determine whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were an explicit focus versus a comparator.

classification.summary: No abstract was available; the title reported incidence of treatment-emergent symptoms under chlorpromazine and placebo conditions, but details were insufficient to judge whether placebo/nocebo was the study focus.

title: Conditioning under carbolonium bromide and D--tubocurarine chloride paralysis.
abstract: The findings of past research using d-tubocurarine chloride as a control procedure in heart rate conditioning have been equivocal. The present experiment compared classical heart rate conditioning under neuromuscular blockade by d-tubocurarine chloride, and a pharmacologically more specific blocker, carbolonium bromide. Both groups were compared to a placebo condition. The results indicated that carbolonium bromide and placebo treated animals acquired deceleratory cardiac conditional responses, but animals treated with d-tubocurarine chloride did not. Unconditional acceleratory responses were found in groups. The findings were discussed in relation to classical conditioning and the psychopharmacology of neuromuscular blockade.

screening.rationale: Empirical animal experiment that tested classical conditioning under neuromuscular blockade with a placebo comparison and reported conditioned responses in the placebo-treated group, so it studies placebo-related responses and conditioning mechanisms.

classification.summary: Compared classical heart-rate conditioning in rats under two neuromuscular blockers and a placebo condition and found that carbolonium and placebo-treated animals acquired deceleratory conditioned cardiac responses while d-tubocurarine-treated animals did not.
classification.key_finding: Carbolonium-treated and placebo-treated rats showed deceleratory conditioned heart-rate responses, whereas d-tubocurarine-treated rats failed to acquire these responses.

title: Clients' treatment expectations at a community mental health center.
abstract: Clients' expectations about mental health care, particularly differences in these expectations as a function of social class, and the relationship of discrepancies between expectations and perceptions to treatment outcome, is examined in this study with 317 Caucasian clients. In contrast to the majority of studies, no differences in treatment expectations relating to clients' social class, sex, or marital status were found. Nor were discrepancies related to course or outcome of therapy. Discussion focuses around explanation and interpretation of these findings. Particularly relevant is the need to determine the extent to which nonusers in the community share the attitudes and expectations of clients.

screening.rationale: Empirical study whose primary focus was patients' treatment expectations and their relation to therapy outcome, which pertains to placebo/expectation science (placebo_science_other).

classification.summary: Examined 317 community mental health clients' treatment expectations and their relation to therapy outcome, and found no differences by social class, sex, or marital status and no relation between expectation–perception discrepancies and outcome.
classification.key_finding: Found no association between expectations or expectation–perception discrepancies and therapy course or outcome.

title: Effects of set on subjects interpretation of placebo marihuana effects.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH indicate the study experimentally manipulated 'set' (expectation) regarding placebo marijuana, making placebo effects the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Investigated how subjects' set (expectation) altered their interpretation of placebo marijuana effects in a randomized trial.

title: Richard C. Cabot--some reflections on deception and placebos in the practice of medicine.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses deception and placebos in medical practice, indicating a commentary on placebo ethics/use which meets 'placebo_science_other' inclusion.

classification.summary: Commentary reflecting on deception and the use of placebos in clinical medical practice.

title: Dextroamphetamine and placebo practice effects on selective attention in hyperactive children.
abstract: Three groups of boys referred to a hospital study unit for evaluation of hyperactive behavior were tested on a classification task involving selective attention while on either dextroamphetamine (D) or placebo (P). In two sessions, groups had D first, P second (DP), or PD, or PP. Amphetamine reduces a response times in general and reduces interference due to orthogonally varying irrelevant information. Practice while on placebo improves performance in a subsequent placebo session. Practice while on amphetamine does not, however, improve performance in the subsequent session on placebo. Assessment of the extent of the drug-state-related practice effect is necessary for evaluation of long-term benefits of dextroamphetamine therapy in these children.

screening.rationale: Empirical crossover study that directly analyzed performance changes following placebo versus drug sessions, reporting practice effects in the placebo condition (placebo response/practice was an object of study).

classification.summary: Tested hyperactive boys in a two-session crossover design and found amphetamine reduced reaction times, practice while on placebo improved subsequent placebo-session performance, but practice while on amphetamine did not transfer to placebo.
classification.key_finding: Amphetamine reduced response times and interference, and practice effects occurred when practice was performed on placebo but not when practiced on amphetamine.

title: Word association times, felt effects, and personality characteristics of science students given a placebo energizer.

screening.rationale: Title indicates an empirical study administering an inert 'placebo energizer' and measuring felt effects, reaction times, and personality—placebo response was the explicit focus (single-group placebo study).

classification.summary: Gave science students an inert 'energizer' and measured word-association reaction times, self-reported felt effects, and personality correlates to study placebo responses.

title: Influence of contextual cues on the efficacy of desensitization and a credible placebo in alleviating public speaking anxiety.
journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology

screening.rationale: Title explicitly tested contextual cues and a credible placebo's efficacy for public-speaking anxiety, indicating placebo/context effects were a study focus (experimental clinical trial).

classification.summary: Studied how contextual cues influenced the effectiveness of desensitization and a credible placebo for public-speaking anxiety.

title: Therapeutic electrical stimulation. The transistorized placebo?
abstract: (1) Electrical stimulation therapy for patients suffering with labile signs and symptoms, and these include all varieties of acute and chronic pains, seizures and spasticity, has come into fashion and gone, and come again with each new technological advance for the past two hundred years. (2) A proportion of patients with chronic disease have their suffering made worse if they feel deprived of the latest therapy and may be relieved if they are given it in the right circumstances. In this group the relief will usually be temporary and the limited supply of such reactors will promote the cycle of fashion. In a group of 126 patients with chronic pain associated with organic disease who were offered transcutaneous stimulation, only 23 (18%) continued to use it one year after they started. (3) The cycling of therapeutic fashion is assisted not only because relief is often temporary, but also by the difficulty in establishing the normal range of variability from which significant change can be assessed and by the uncertain relationship between signs and symptoms and for the functions of daily living. For these reasons there is an inevitable tendency to temporary over-optimism and it seems impossible to counter this by the execution of a satisfactory clinical trial, since the patient cannot be "blind" and a significant variable is the enthusiasm with which a therapy is surrounded. (4) Electrical stimulation by cutaneous devices or implants can give much benefit to some patients in whom other methods have failed and there are indications, not only from anecdote and clinical impression but also now from experimental physiology, that it may benefit by mechanisms of interaction at the first sensory synapse. It is, however, an over-simplification to regard any therapy as either strictly physiological or simply fraudulent. Like other so-called placebos, physical methods of therapy can presumably act on hormonal systems associated with stress and the experience of pain.

screening.rationale: Narrative/historical article whose main topic was therapeutic electrical stimulation and the placebo/ritual/contextual mechanisms and observations about placebo-like responses.

classification.summary: Reviewed the history and cycling of electrical stimulation therapies, discussed placebo-like contextual and hormonal mechanisms, and reported that of 126 chronic pain patients offered transcutaneous stimulation only 23 (18%) continued use at one year.
classification.key_finding: Observed that 18% (23/126) of chronic pain patients continued transcutaneous stimulation one year after starting.

title: Clinical correlants of changes in nasal flow/resistance (Rn) measurements.
abstract: It has been suggested that changes in nasal airways flow/resistance imply clinical betterment and increased nasal patency, and that patients with congestion sense relief when treatment improves their Rn values by 20% or more, speculations supported by inferences from lower airways dynamics. This hypothesis was tested in a double-blind study of the nasal decongestant potency of phenylpropanolamine/aromatic oil, phenilpropanolamine, aromatic oil and placebo syrups given to 80 patients with common colds who were followed for 6 hours. Rn was determined by electronic posterior rhinometry; patients estimated their degree of nasal congestion with a 6-ranked subjective scale. Statistical techniques included paired and unpaired t-tests, chi-square analysis, analysis of covariance to determine comparisons of within-group differences, differences between drug and placebo groups, and determination of the number in each group improving 20% or more from control Rn. Correlation coefficients relating Rn values to subjective responses were determined by pairing these for each patient and applying standard regression analysis. Despite a strong placebo effect, mean Rn changes ranked the efficacy of the 4 test mixtures, with the 20% improvement criterion allowing the sharpest separation of active mixtures from inactive. In regression analysis the correlation coefficient of 0.56 and the regression slope of 0.66 were both significant (p = 0.01 or better); the latter figure implied that a 1 unit difference on the subjective scale corresponded to a 0.66 unit difference on the Rn scale. With an average objective reading of 3.77 a 1 unit change n the subjective rating perceptible to the subject as a difference in the state of his nasal congestion was equivalent to a mean Rn change of 17.5%. This supports our prior assumption, indicating that a 17.5% to 20% improvement in Rn is experienced as clinical relief. Further, subjective rating scales appear to be statistically sound as a means of assessment of the status of the nasal airways.

screening.rationale: Randomized, double-blind trial reported a strong placebo response and analyzed placebo-arm changes and correlations between subjective relief and objective nasal resistance, meeting criteria for placebo_response inclusion.

classification.summary: Tested phenylpropanolamine/aromatic oil, components, and placebo in a double-blind RCT (n=80) for 6 hours and found correlated objective Rn improvements and subjective nasal relief, noting a strong placebo response and ~17.5–20% Rn change as perceptible relief.
classification.key_finding: Found a significant correlation (r=0.56, p≤0.01) between objective Rn change and subjective congestion ratings, with ~17.5–20% Rn improvement corresponding to perceptible relief; a notable placebo response was present.

title: Placebo effect in the treatment of angina pectoris.
abstract: The interference of placebo effect in the treatment of angina pectoris has been studied in a group of patients with stable angina pectoris, selected on the basis of normal electrocardiogram at rest and a pathologic ergometric electrocardiographic test. It was found that the patients could be divided, according to the results of the exercise test, into two groups: placebo responders and place-bo-non-responders. The anti-anginal effect of beta-blocking agents has been clearly demonstrated only in the placebo-non-responders group. No statistically significant effect of beta-blocking agents was observed in the placebo-responders group. This result shows that it is necessary, in double blind trials, at first to separate placebo-responders from placebo-non responders. Otherwise the correct evaluation of a drug can be modified by the placebo-responders group.

screening.rationale: Study explicitly analyzed placebo responders versus non-responders in a double-blind trial of angina and evaluated drug effects by placebo-response status, making placebo response the analytic focus.

classification.summary: Analyzed patients with stable angina in a double-blind trial, identified placebo responders and non-responders, and found beta-blocker benefit only in placebo non-responders.
classification.key_finding: Beta-blocking agents produced clear anti-anginal effects in placebo-non-responders but not in placebo-responders.

title: The effect of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TNS) on joint pain in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: The effect of transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS) on joint pain was studied in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Three different forms of TNS were used in an attempt to evaluate the influence of placebo effects. The results were evaluated by means of loading tests and from the patients' own assessments of pain relief. High intensity TNS near the painful joint gave pain relief of varying degree in 95% of the patients, while TNS of low intensity and TNS applied at a remote site gave an improvement in 75% and 5% respectively. It seems quite clear that TNS is effective in reducing joint pain. There are a number of factors which intimate that this improvement is not merely a placebo effect.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial explicitly compared different TNS intensities/sites to evaluate and isolate placebo-like (sham) effects, making placebo phenomena an explicit focus.

classification.summary: Randomized trial tested three TNS variants in rheumatoid arthritis and reported greater pain relief with high-intensity local TNS than low-intensity or remote-site (sham) stimulation, aiming to evaluate placebo effects.
classification.key_finding: High-intensity local TNS produced pain relief in ~95% of patients versus 75% for low-intensity and 5% for remote-site sham, suggesting specific efficacy beyond placebo.

title: Health care: no time for placebos.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available and the title suggests a historical/commentary piece about placebos but it's unclear whether placebo/nocebo is the explicit focus required for inclusion.

classification.summary: Appeared to discuss the role or history of placebos in healthcare in the United States, but no abstract or text was available to confirm focus or findings.

title: The functional relationship between artificial food colors and hyperactivity.
abstract: The presence of a functional relationship between the ingestion of artificial food colors and an increase in the frequency and/or duration of selected behaviors that are representative of the hyperactive behavior syndrome was experimentally investigated. Two eight-year-old females, who had been on the Feingold K-P diet for a minimum of 11 months, were the subjects studied. The experimental design was a variation of the BAB design, with double-blind conditions. This design allowed an experimental analysis of the placebo phases as well as challenge phases. Data were obtained by trained observers on Out of Seat, On Task, and Physically Aggressive behaviors, as they occurred in the subjects' regular class setting. Results indicated (a) the existence of a functional relationship between the ingestion of artificial food colors and an increase in both the duration and frequency of hyperactive behaviors, (b) the absence of a placebo effect, and (c) differential sensitivity of the dependent variables to the challenge effects.

screening.rationale: Experimental within-subject double-blind BAB design explicitly analyzed placebo phases and reported presence/absence of placebo effect, so placebo phenomena were an explicit focus (experimental placebo/challenge comparison).

classification.summary: Studied two 8-year-old girls in a double-blind BAB design and found artificial food colors increased observed hyperactive behaviors while no placebo effect was observed.
classification.key_finding: Found that ingestion of artificial food colors increased frequency and duration of hyperactive behaviors and that there was an absence of a placebo effect.

title: Double-blind oral analgesic study of butorphanol in episiotomy pain: a comparison with codeine and placebo.
journal: The Journal of international medical research

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and the title/metadata indicate a drug efficacy RCT with a placebo arm but do not reveal whether the paper analyzed the placebo response/effect itself.

classification.summary: No abstract available; randomized double-blind trial compared oral butorphanol, codeine, and placebo for episiotomy pain in adults.

title: Man, magic and the modern placebo.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the paper addresses placebo, physician-patient relations and communication as its primary subject (theory/commentary), so it meets inclusion as placebo-science content.

classification.summary: Discusses the concept of the placebo in modern medicine, emphasizing physician-patient communication, cultural/ritual aspects, and the role of belief in therapeutic outcomes.

title: Doctors, physiotherapists, and placebo pharmacology.
abstract: A seminar of physiotherapists studied the psychological aspects of their work. Difficulty with doctors rather than patients was unexpectedly prominent. The following factors were identified as contributing to their dissatisfaction: doctors misused physiotherapy as a placebo in cases of incurable and untreatable disease and mental problems; because they faced questions about diagnosis and prognosis that doctors escaped they learnt to avoid knowing the facts about their patients; using quasiscientific apparatus had tended to replace physical contact; they saw their psychological skill as illicit and unprofessional; and they were uncertain about their role as social workers. Nevertheless, they tended to idealise doctors, which sharpened gratification in collaborative work and helped to alleviate anxiety about death and disease, but tended to reinforce sexual stereotyping and the image of physiotherapy as "unscientific," empirical, and intuititive ("feminine").

screening.rationale: Paper reported a seminar study of physiotherapists' attitudes about use of physiotherapy as a placebo and ethical/role issues, fitting 'placebo science' (attitudes/ethics) inclusion.

classification.summary: Reported a seminar of physiotherapists who discussed that doctors sometimes used physiotherapy as a placebo and described related role, ethical, and interpersonal issues.

title: Smoking treatment strategies, expectancy outcomes, and credibility in attention-placebo control conditions.
abstract: Assessed credibility of the rapid smoking procedure, covert sensitization a combined approach, satiation, and a relaxation technique in a group of 38 self-reported cigarette smokers. The results suggested that while sex is not a factor in credibility ratings, different treatment strategies do elicit varying degrees of confidence in terms of positive treatment expectances. Scheffé's method of posttest comparisons revealed that satiation was least preferred, while the relaxation procedure was rated the highest in credibility. The other aversive treatment strategies did not differ significantly from either the relaxation or satiation procedures. These findings are discussed as they relate to credibility as a nonspecific treatment variable that smoking researchers may effectively manipulate through a rating procedure in creating a more sound experimental design in attention-placebo control conditions.

screening.rationale: Study empirically measured credibility/expectancy of treatment and attention-placebo control procedures, addressing placebo-related methodological variables.

classification.summary: Assessed credibility ratings of several smoking-treatment and attention-placebo procedures in 38 smokers and found differences in expectancies, with relaxation rated highest and satiation lowest.
classification.key_finding: Relaxation received the highest credibility ratings and satiation the lowest; sex did not affect credibility.
